analysis.one_liner: Allows importing FDA-approved prescription drugs and shields legal Internet pharmacies from federal action.
analysis.headline: The Prescription Drug Affordability Act died in committee without a vote, cosponsor, or committee action in the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Ron Paul's bill would repeal the federal restrictions that currently bar importing prescription drugs from abroad. It would let anyone apply to import FDA-approved drugs, and HHS would have to approve qualified applications within 60 days. It also bars the federal government from acting against Internet pharmacy sales that comply with federal and state law and post accurate compliance information. It never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially those without insurance coverage or with high copays, who could buy FDA-approved versions of the same drugs at the lower prices charged overseas. Legal Internet pharmacies that sell compliantly would gain clear federal protection against enforcement actions.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that restrict importing prescription drugs, letting qualified persons import FDA-approved drugs even if they are not the drug's manufacturer.
Requires the HHS Secretary to approve import applications, within 60 days, for drugs that are FDA-approved and not adulterated or misbranded.
Bars federal action against Internet sales of prescription drugs that comply with federal and state law and post accurate compliance information on the site.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose ability to charge higher US prices depends in part on keeping cheaper foreign versions of FDA-approved drugs out of the US market. Federal agencies would also bear the cost of processing import applications and setting up a new regulatory system.

drawbacks.text: Opening personal and commercial importation, especially through websites, creates channels for counterfeit, mishandled, or improperly stored drugs to reach consumers, a risk FDA has historically cited in opposing drug importation.

The bill's compliance-and-posting requirement relies on sellers self-reporting that their sales follow federal and state law, which puts the burden of verifying safety and legality largely on consumers.

Savings would be limited to drugs that are FDA-approved in the same form, and patent rights are explicitly preserved, so brand-name drugs still under patent could remain unavailable from cheaper foreign sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — letting Americans buy FDA-approved drugs at the lower prices charged abroad — offers real savings to consumers at real cost to drug makers' US pricing. The bill carries genuine safety and enforcement risks in Internet sales, but it does not erode patents and keeps the FDA-approval and non-adulteration requirements in place. On balance it is a consumer-friendly bill whose main weakness is underdeveloped oversight of Internet sellers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee and sat there until the Congress ended, never reaching a committee vote or the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability Act on January 5, 2011.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and to the Subcommittee on Health on February 1, 2011.
No further action was taken; the bill drew no cosponsors and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical makers kept the import restrictions that protect their US pricing structure, and consumers got no new path to cheaper foreign versions of FDA-approved drugs.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 5, 2011, sent it to the Health Subcommittee on February 1, 2011, and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Fought importation legislation across multiple Congresses, arguing imported drugs posed safety risks; the import restrictions this bill repeals remain in force.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsor was a conservative Republican and it drew no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed on the record.

industries.note: Importation of FDA-approved drugs would expose the US market to lower foreign prices, undermining the higher prices drug makers charge Americans. Their industry has consistently opposed such bills; the repeal never happened.

The bill would shield compliant Internet sellers from federal enforcement and would create importation business that today is barred. Consumers could face more counterfeit-drug risk, but the bill conditions the shield on legal compliance.
Retail pharmacies could lose prescription volume to imported and Internet alternatives, but large players could also become licensed importers themselves.
